title: Hershele and Market Day
summary: On market day in Mezhibozh, everyone is waiting for Hershele with a question: the baker, the tailor, the shoemaker, the water-carrier and even old Reb Yossel, who offers a whole challah to whoever can catch him out. But every time, Hershele has a quick answer, smiles, and vanishes among the stalls. A funny rhyming story about quick wits, with a repeating line that is fun to shout.
pages:
Market day in Mezhibozh! Everyone stood by their stalls,
and the merchants whispered: "Hershele's coming today! We'll catch him — we're ready, one and all!"
And then he arrived: a patched green hat, and mischievous eyes,
and a smile that said: "Ask, ask away — I've got replies!"

The baker asked: "Which is better, Hershele — one big challah or two small?"
"Two big ones!" answered Hershele, and the baker wondered: "Why didn't I think of big ones at all?"
The baker stood with his mouth wide open, and the merchants were grinning, one and all,
and Hershele smiled, and vanished among the stalls.

The tailor pointed at Hershele's hat: "So many holes! How come the rain doesn't soak you through?"
"It comes in one hole and goes out the other — like a friendly guest just passing through!"
The tailor froze with his needle in the air, his eyes as round as balls,
and Hershele smiled, and vanished among the stalls.

The shoemaker pointed: "Your shoes are so big! How don't you fall? How don't you trip?"
"Slowly!" said Hershele. "We're still getting acquainted — soon we'll be friends, and more, a real friendship..."
The shoemaker put down his hammer and kept a straight face, as if it wasn't funny at all,
and Hershele smiled, and vanished among the stalls.

The water-carrier asked: "And what if I pour a bucket of water on you?"
"Then thank you!" said Hershele. "I haven't had a bath in two years — it's long overdue!"
The water-carrier stood holding his bucket, and the merchants felt a lot less ready, after all,
and Hershele smiled, and vanished among the stalls.

Reb Yossel set a big challah on the table, warm and shiny, whole and round,
and called: "Whoever catches Hershele with a question — this challah's his! Here it is! No tricks — fair and sound!"

Reb Yossel asked, smoothing his mustache: "Tell me, Hershele, when do we say the blessing on the moon?"
"I'm not from here!" answered Hershele. "I'm from Ostropol. Over here — who knows, maybe your moon ran off too soon?"
Reb Yossel looked up at the sky, where the moon smiled with half a face above them all,
and Hershele smiled, and vanished among the stalls.

Rivka the fish-seller laughed: "On Shabbat we get an extra soul! And you — how many souls do you have? Do tell!"
"One," said Hershele. "So that's the extra one. And on weekdays — I manage without a soul just as well!"
And the fish in her stall gaped with open mouths, as still as stones, one and all,
and Hershele smiled, and vanished among the stalls.

A little boy in a kippah tugged at Hershele's sleeve:
"How do you know all the answers, every one?"
"I don't know them!" whispered Hershele. "I just smile — and here they come!"

Now everyone asked at once: the baker, the tailor, the shoemaker, and the water-carrier too:
"Who? And what? And when? And how?" — and Hershele smiled: "Please — two at a time, not all of you!"

Reb Yossel lifted the challah and said: "We couldn't catch you with questions — that's clear!
So take the challah, and leave us another story here!"
"I'm caught! — but by a challah, and that doesn't count!" And he broke it up for everyone, and the whole market cheered.
The merchants waved to him from far away, with challah in hand and smiles for all,
and Hershele smiled, and vanished among the stalls.
